---
title: "Python interface for solvers"
---

The package gives lovejx, G-ADOPT and any other solver one way to read what a
case prescribes and one way to hold and score what the solver produced. None
of it computes a response.

## One entry point

```python
import giamip

case = giamip.case("martinec2018-B")   # MartinecCase
case = giamip.case("spada2011-t02-01") # SpadaCase
case = giamip.case("giamip-exp01")     # GiamipExperiment
```

The case files are in the package. The data files are not: a reader gets each
one through `giamip.data.locate`, which downloads it from data.gadopt.org on
first use and caches it ([Fetching the data](../data/fetching.qmd)). Every
NetCDF file is read and written through h5netcdf, on h5py, which applies no
mask, scale or fill value.

## Martinec (2018): setting up a case

`giamip.benchmarks.inputs.MartinecCase` reads the case file, the load table
and the earth model, and evaluates the load and the topography at the points
a solver chooses.

```python
from giamip.benchmarks.inputs import MartinecCase

case = MartinecCase("D")
case.earth_layers()                          # radii, densities, moduli, viscosities
case.ice_density, case.water_density         # 931 and 1000 kg/m3
h = case.ice_thickness(colat, lon, t_kyr)    # the cap, in metres, at any points
grid = case.ice_on_grid(lat_north_first, lon, times_kyr)   # (times, lat, lon)
zeta = case.topography(colat, lon)           # the basin, eq. 29
case.topography_time                         # "initial", or "terminal" for case E
case.profiles, case.time_series              # what to output and compare
```

The cap is the square-root profile of Spada et al. (2011). In scenario T1 the
height and the radius grow together and the profile stays the same shape; the
total mass then equals VEGA's to 2e-4 at every time, which a test checks.

## Martinec (2018): results and scores

`giamip.benchmarks.results.BenchmarkResult` holds the curves of one code for
one case, in the same layout as the converted reference files, so a solver's
output and a published contributor are read, plotted and scored the same way.

```python
from giamip.benchmarks.results import BenchmarkResult
from giamip.benchmarks import metrics

run = BenchmarkResult("D", "lovejx")
run.add_profile("load", "U", colatitude_deg, u_m)
run.add_time_series("h_UF", time_kyr, h_uf_m)
run.write("outputs/martinec2018/lovejx/martinec2018-D.nc")
BenchmarkResult.read("outputs/martinec2018/lovejx/martinec2018-D.nc", "lovejx")

reference = BenchmarkResult.reference("D")      # the curves scoring compares with
shipped = BenchmarkResult.reference("D", "ZM")  # VEGA's files as the archive has them
case = MartinecCase("D")
case.reference_colatitudes("basin")             # VEGA's own points, if you want them

metrics.score(run)                              # eq. 31 per profile and time series
metrics.envelope_check(run, band_half_width_deg=6.74)   # criterion 2
metrics.uniform_layer("D")                      # h_UF of the reference, S - N
```

The reference is VEGA. `BenchmarkResult.reference(case)` reads the group
`reference` of the converted file, which the converter builds by the rule of
the case file's `reference_data.reference_curves`: VEGA as shipped, or VEGA
recovered as YS's profile minus YS's own difference file, where the shipped
file is not the one the published differences were computed against (case A,
the case B basin and case D). Each curve's attributes say how it was built,
and [the protocol page](../protocol/martinec2018.qmd) gives the evidence.

`metrics.score` compares a profile on the result's own points inside the
colatitude interval of the case file, with the reference evaluated there by a
cubic spline, so a solver can sample at any points. Scored this way, every
contributor of the archive gets the numbers of its own published difference
file. A time series is compared on the result's own times, with the reference
interpolated linearly. Each row carries the number of points, the largest
spacing between them, how the reference was built and the giamip version.

`metrics.envelope_check` is criterion 2 of the G-ADOPT tests: the result's
largest difference and RMS against the largest of the published codes, with a
band removed around the cap margin and the initial coastline
(`MartinecCase.feature_colatitudes`). The band width has no default, because
it is not decided. The function raises when the result lacks a compared
curve.

## Using giamip in a solver's benchmark test

This section is for the agent or person who adds a Martinec benchmark to a
solver's own test suite, as G-ADOPT does in `tests/gia_selfgrav_benchmarks/`.
It needs only `pip install giamip` in the solver's environment.

### What a result must hold

A result holds the curves the case file compares, in SI units, with the signs
and datums of [the conventions](conventions.qmd): U, N and S in metres,
positive upward; `h_UF` in metres; ice masses in kg; the ocean area as a
fraction of 4π. The table is generated from the case files, and a solver
reads the same lists from `case.profiles` and `case.time_series`.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path("../..").resolve()))
from IPython.display import Markdown
import giamip

rows = ["| Case | Profiles: meridian, quantities, interval | Time series, 0 to 15 kyr | Terminal time |",
        "| --- | --- | --- | ---: |"]
for letter in "ABCDE":
    case = giamip.case(f"martinec2018-{letter}")
    profiles = "; ".join(f"{p.name} (longitude {p.longitude_deg:g}): {', '.join(p.quantities)}, "
                         f"{p.colatitude_interval_deg[0]:g} to {p.colatitude_interval_deg[1]:g} degrees"
                         for p in case.profiles) or "none"
    series = ", ".join(q for s in case.time_series for q in s.quantities) or "none"
    rows.append(f"| {letter} | {profiles} | {series} | {case.terminal_time_kyr:g} kyr |")
Markdown("\n".join(rows))
```

A solver may sample a profile at any colatitudes. Scoring evaluates the
reference at the result's own points, and the result must reach to within 1
per cent of the interval's width at each end. Each score row reports
`max_spacing`, so a grid too coarse to see a peak shows. For VEGA's own
points, call `case.reference_colatitudes(profile)`; this reads the reference
file, so on a machine with no network the cache must hold it.

### The two stages

A benchmark on a cluster has two stages: the run on the compute nodes, and the
test that reads the run afterwards. The example below is complete. It runs
in `tests/test_doc_examples.py`, with `my_profile` and `my_series` replaced by
a stand-in that returns the reference, so it cannot go out of date.

```python
# example: solver benchmark test
import numpy as np
import giamip
from giamip.benchmarks import metrics
from giamip.benchmarks.results import BenchmarkResult

# ---- stage 1, the run (compute node; needs no data file and no network) ----
case = giamip.case("martinec2018-C")
rho_ice, rho_water, g = case.ice_density, case.water_density, case.surface_gravity
# The load and the topography at the solver's own points, at any time:
#   case.ice_thickness(colatitude_deg, longitude_deg, t_kyr), case.topography(...)
# ... the solver runs here ...
run = BenchmarkResult(case.letter, "my-code")
for profile in case.profiles:
    for quantity in profile.quantities:
        colatitude_deg, values_m = my_profile(profile, quantity)
        run.add_profile(profile.name, quantity, colatitude_deg, values_m)
for series in case.time_series:
    for quantity in series.quantities:
        time_kyr, values = my_series(quantity)
        run.add_time_series(quantity, time_kyr, values)
run.write(output_dir / "martinec2018-C.nc")        # output_dir: a pathlib.Path of yours

# ---- stage 2, the test (login node or laptop; the reference is fetched) ----
run = BenchmarkResult.read(output_dir / "martinec2018-C.nc", "my-code", case="C")
rows = case.score(run)                                        # eq. 31, one row per curve
checks = case.envelope_check(run, band_half_width_deg=6.74)   # criterion 2
assert all(row["inside"] for row in checks), checks
reference_h_uf, spread = metrics.uniform_layer("C")           # S - N of the reference
series = run.series("h_UF")
ours = float(np.interp(case.terminal_time_kyr, series.axis, series.values))
assert abs(ours - reference_h_uf) <= 0.01 * abs(reference_h_uf)   # the solver's tolerance
vega = case.reference().series("ice_mass_grounded")           # VEGA's series
```

giamip gives the metrics and the range of the published codes. The pass
tolerances (1 per cent above) belong to the solver's test. The band width of
criterion 2 is a required argument because it is not decided; 6.74 degrees is
the width of the first G-ADOPT verdicts.

### On Gadi

The compute-node stage needs the package and nothing else. The test stage
reads the converted reference files. A login node has network access, so the
first test run downloads them into the download root. To keep them in one
place for every job and every user of a project, set `GIAMIP_DATA_ROOT` to a
directory on `/g/data`, and fill it once:

```bash
GIAMIP_DATA_ROOT=/g/data/<project>/giamip python -m giamip.data --stage converted --collection benchmarks
```

The Firedrake module must have giamip installed with h5netcdf and
`packaging`; h5py, numpy and scipy are there. See
[Fetching the data](../data/fetching.qmd).

### Moving from a giamip checkout to the package

Code written against a checkout on `sys.path` (the variable `GIA_MIP`)
changes as follows.

| With a checkout | With the package |
| --- | --- |
| `GIA_MIP` and `sys.path.insert(...)` | `pip install giamip`; plain imports |
| reading `cases/benchmarks/martinec2018/<L>.json` and `loads/martinec2018.json` with `json.load` | `giamip.case("martinec2018-<L>")`. The files moved to `giamip/resources/`, so old paths fail |
| `spec["sea_level_equation"]`, `["terminal_time_kyr"]`, `["ice_height_model"]`, `["time_scenario"]`, `["ocean_basin"]` | `case.sea_level_equation`, `case.terminal_time_kyr`, `case.ice_height_model`, `case.time_scenario`, `case.ocean_basin` |
| `constants.ice_density_kg_m3`, `water_density_kg_m3`, `surface_gravity_m_s2` | `case.ice_density`, `case.water_density`, `case.surface_gravity` |
| `ice_height_models[...]`, `load_shape.angular_radius_deg` | `case.cap` (centre, `height_m`, `radius_deg`); `case.cap_size(t_kyr)` for T1 |
| `time_scenarios[...].growth_end_kyr` | `case.load_table["time_scenarios"][case.time_scenario].get("growth_end_kyr")` |
| `ocean_basins[...]`, `sigma_b_deg` | `case.basin` (centre, `bmax_m`, `b0_m`, `sigma_b_deg`); `case.basin_radius_deg()` |
| a JSON copy of the VEGA colatitudes | any points; or `case.reference_colatitudes(profile)` |
| `.npz` files and `scripts/martinec_gadopt.read_run` | `BenchmarkResult.add_profile`, `add_time_series`, `write`; `BenchmarkResult.read` |
| `scripts/martinec_compare.score(values, reference, colatitude, interval)` (one dict) | `metrics.score(result)` or `case.score(result)` (a list of rows) |
| a hand-written band and contributor bar for criterion 2 | `case.envelope_check(result, band_half_width_deg=...)`; `case.feature_colatitudes(profile)` |
| `report_uniform_layer(result, letter)` | `metrics.uniform_layer(letter)` against the run's `h_UF` at the terminal time |
| `BenchmarkResult.reference(letter, "ZM")` | unchanged for VEGA as shipped; `BenchmarkResult.reference(letter)` or `case.reference()` for the curves scoring uses |

Two numbers move when a solver switches. The case B basin and both case D
profiles are scored against VEGA recovered on 2048 points, not the 359-row
shipped file; at the shipped rows the two agree to 7e-5 m or better, and
between them the old linear interpolation was off by up to 0.24 m. The
feature colatitudes come from the geometry (75.1497, 124.8503, 10.1497,
59.8503 degrees) where earlier code typed 75.15, 124.85, 10.149 and 59.849, so
one grid point can cross a band edge.

## Spada (2011): setting up a test

`giamip.benchmarks.inputs.SpadaCase` reads the case file, the load table
`giamip/resources/loads/spada2011.json` and the earth model. It gives the three loads as surface
density and as Legendre coefficients, and the epochs, grids and degrees to
output.

```python
from giamip.benchmarks.inputs import SpadaCase

case = SpadaCase("t02-01")
case.earth_layers()                          # M3-L70-V01, or VSS96 in test 6/1
case.ice_density, case.water_density         # 931 and 1000 kg/m3, from the load table
case.loads                                   # ("cap", "disc", "point")
case.load_centre                             # (0.0, 0.0), or (25.0, 75.0) in test 3/2
case.load_mass("cap")                        # 3.607171340900778e18 kg
sigma = case.surface_density("disc", theta)  # kg/m2 at an angle from the load centre
sigma_n = case.legendre_coefficients("cap", range(0, 129))   # kg/m2
case.epochs_kyr                              # (0, 1, 2, 5, 10, inf)
case.harmonic_degrees                        # (2, 128)
case.near_field_colatitudes_deg()            # 0 to 25 at 0.25 degree
case.global_colatitudes_deg()                # 0 to 180 at 1 degree
case.outputs                                 # ["U", "V", "N"]
```

The cap is the square-root profile, and its coefficients satisfy
sigma(theta) = sum_n sigma_n P_n(cos theta), so 4 pi a^2 sigma_0 is the load mass.
The fluid limit is `math.inf`, which is a different epoch from 1000 kyr.

## Spada (2011): results and scores

`giamip.benchmarks.results.SpadaResult` holds one code's results for one test,
in the layout of the converted reference files: Love numbers (elastic, fluid
and residues per mode), the relaxation spectrum, Love numbers against time,
the polar motion transfer function, U, V, N or their rates, polar motion and
the length of day.

```python
from giamip.benchmarks.results import SpadaResult
from giamip.benchmarks import metrics

run = SpadaResult("t01-02", "lovejx")
run.add_love_numbers("h", degrees, elastic, fluid, residues)   # residues (degrees, 9), 1/kyr
run.write("outputs/spada2011/lovejx/spada2011-t01-02.nc")

run = SpadaResult("t02-01", "lovejx")
run.add_spatial("cap", "U", 10.0, colatitude_deg, u_m)
run.add_spatial("cap", "U", math.inf, colatitude_deg, u_fluid_m)

path = SpadaResult.reference_path("t02-01")   # located, and downloaded on first use
references = {m: SpadaResult.read(path, m) for m in SpadaResult.members(path)}
metrics.spada_score(run, references)          # rows per contributor, near field and whole meridian
```

Residues follow the convention of the paper, h_f = h_e - sum_j r_j / s_j, and
mode 1 is the slowest mode, the s_j closest to zero. Rates are in m/kyr, which
is the same number as mm/yr. The paper has no reference code, so
`spada_score` scores against each contributor separately and names it in every
row. An epoch is compared only when both results hold it exactly, so a fluid
limit is never compared with GS's run at 1000 kyr.

Tests 5/1 to 7/1, 4/1 and 3/2 use four further kinds of result.

```python
run = SpadaResult("t01-05", "lovejx")
run.add_time_domain_love_numbers("h", 2, time_kyr, h_t)        # one curve per quantity and degree

run = SpadaResult("t01-04", "lovejx")
run.add_polar_motion_transfer_function("included", a_e, a_s, frequencies, residues)
                                                               # complex, 1/kyr; A_e dimensionless

run = SpadaResult("t02-03", "lovejx")
run.add_polar_motion("cap", "excluded", "m_x", time_kyr, m_x_deg)
run.add_polar_motion("cap", "excluded", "m_rate_modulus", time_kyr, rate_deg_per_myr)
run.add_length_of_day("cap", time_kyr, delta_lod_ms)
```

The Chandler wobble setting is `"included"` or `"excluded"`. Polar motion is
in degrees and its rate in degrees per Myr, the units of table 14. The modes of
the transfer function are stored slowest first, by the real part of a_j.

`spada_score` compares Love numbers against time in log10 of time, over the
time window of the case file where it gives one. It compares polar motion and
the length of day linearly in time over the whole reference. With the Chandler
wobble included, polar motion oscillates with a period of about 1.2 years, and
the reference files sample it once a year. A solver result must therefore hold
the reference's own times for that comparison to mean anything. The transfer
function scores A_e and A_s, and scores the modes only when both results hold
the same number of modes. GS holds three Maxwell modes that VB does not hold.

## GIAMIP: inputs

`giamip.mip.inputs.GiamipExperiment` opens the ice history and the topography
an experiment prescribes, through h5netcdf, which applies no mask, with the
grid checked and the corrections for the version of the file on disk. The
files are located through `giamip.data.locate`, so they are downloaded and
unpacked on first use (361 MB for the ice histories).

```python
from giamip.mip.inputs import GiamipExperiment, grounded_thickness

exp = GiamipExperiment("Exp01")
ice = exp.ice_history                       # IceHistory
ice.years                                   # years from 2000 CE
h = ice.thickness(step, north_first=True)   # (257, 513), metres
bed = exp.topography.elevation(north_first=True)
steps = exp.forcing_steps()                 # the steps inside the period; Exp06 and Exp07 read the _80ka files
grounded = grounded_thickness(h, bed, exp.constants["ice_density_kg_m3"],
                              exp.constants["ocean_water_density_kg_m3"])
```

The GIAMIP grid has 257 latitudes and 513 longitudes. A solver that assumes
`nlat` by `2 nlat` longitudes, as the lovejx sea-level solver does, cannot take
it without regridding.

## GIAMIP: earth structure

`giamip.earth` gives the radial earth of an experiment at any radius: density,
bulk and shear modulus, wave speeds, gravity and viscosity. It reads the
elastic structure, PREM-stable for every 1D experiment, from its node table and
the viscosity structure from its model file. Every column of the node table is
interpolated linearly in radius, which is the rule of protocol v4.0 Section 3.1
for density. The viscosity is constant in each layer, infinite in the elastic
lid and NaN in the core. The deepest layer reaches the core-mantle boundary of
the elastic structure.

```python
import numpy as np
import giamip

e = giamip.case("giamip-exp01").earth()     # with the G-ADOPT choices; gadopt=False for the protocol alone
r = np.linspace(3480e3, 6371e3, 2000)       # radii in metres, any shape
v = e(r)                                    # dict of arrays with the shape of r
v["rho_kg_m3"], v["kappa_Pa"], v["mu_Pa"], v["g_m_s2"], v["viscosity_pa_s"]
v = e(r, side="below")                      # on a boundary, the value below it
```

The radii are in metres and every value is in SI units, as the key names say.
At a radius exactly on a boundary of either structure, `side="above"` (the
default) gives the value just above it and `side="below"` the value just below.
With the default, a mantle mesh with nodes on the core-mantle boundary gets
mantle values there. One call is one binary search per radius and no loop in
Python, and the same radii give the same values on every machine.

`e.compressibility` is `compressible` for every G-ADOPT run, and the bulk
modulus is that of the file. Exp08, Exp11 and Exp12 raise
`NotImplementedError`: their G-ADOPT choices vary laterally, and the grids will
come from g-drift.
